title: Lahore, 1765
hookLine: Sikh chiefs entered Lahore and struck coins in the Gurus' names

lines: A COIN TRAVELS FARTHER THAN AN ARMY.
WHOSE NAME GOES ON THE COIN?
cards: Check the coins in a pocket or a purse. Whose face is on them? Whose name?
A coin goes where no army goes: into markets, kitchens and strangers' hands.
So when Sikh chiefs rode into Lahore, the great city where Sikhs had been hunted, tortured and killed, there was an obvious next step, the thing anyone holding a city does. Strike a coin.
The question is whose name to put on it.

teach.h: LAHORE: THE CITY OF THE HARD YEARS.
teach.b: First, the city. Lahore was the seat of governors this path has met in the hard years, with its prisons and its executions. Now Sikh chiefs held it.

teach.h: NO CHIEF'S NAME, THE GURUS' NAMES.
teach.b: Tradition says the coins they struck carried no chief's name. Instead they carried a short verse in Persian, the language of coins and courts, naming Guru Nanak and Guru Gobind Singh.
In the common telling, the verse says that the deg, the teg and the fateh, along with the help that came without delay, were received from Guru Nanak and Guru Gobind Singh.
Third, the three words, which are worth slowing down for. Deg is a big cooking pot, the kind used in the langar, the free kitchen. Teg is a sword.

teach.h: DEG, TEG, FATEH: POT, SWORD, VICTORY.
teach.b: Fateh is victory. So the pot comes before the sword. Feeding people is named first, defending them second, and the victory is credited to the Gurus.
A chief could have stamped his own name and claimed the win. This coin says it wasn't theirs to claim. Fourth, why it matters on an ordinary day.
Whatever people put their name on tells others what they think they own.

teach.h: THE CREDIT GOES PAST THE CHIEFS.
teach.b: Sikhs remember this coin as one that pointed past the people who made it.

how: Coins struck by Sikh rulers in the Gurus' names are kept in museums and collections, and Sikhs still use the phrase deg teg fateh for the ideals of feeding and protecting.

games.q: you're a Sikh chief who has just taken Lahore, the city where your people were hunted. you can strike a coin. whose name do you put on it?
o: your own, so everyone knows who won.
no name at all, just the city.
games.why: tradition says the coins named Guru Nanak and Guru Gobind Singh, and credited the victory to them.

practice: Hold something minted in your palm, a coin, a medal, a stamped key, a banknote, and feel its weight.
Look at what's on it, a face, a name, a motto, and remember someone decided that; then, breathing slowly, ask what you'd want stamped on your own work, if anything, and whose name it would carry.
If you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Lahore. Tradition says that when Sikh chiefs took the city, they struck coins carrying not their own names but the names of Guru Nanak and Guru Gobind Singh. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi for deg teg fateh: the cooking pot, the sword, and victory.

carryVoice: Your line: the gurus' coin. Credit can point past the hand that earned it. See you tomorrow.
